Well in the last installment you found out that I acquired 160 acres of sand, sage brush, rocks and rattle snakes, but very little water.When I took title to the property, it was mid summer so I only got to drive out to it once. But that fall I made it back for a deer hunting trip. I got a buck with out too much trouble. While I was looking around the property i noticed that the little draw that contained entrance into my property had a dried out small stream bed starting about half way down the draw. So I decided that I would return back to the property in the early spring (April 15 or there abouts.) to see if the steam bed carried any water.

Well I made my trip out to my property the next spring and i indeed found a small spring that came out of the rocks about half way down the draw. The past winter was not the best for moisture but the stream flow as about 2 gallons a minute. With that small amount of flow the water barely made it a 100 feet before sinking into the ground. But it was something. My next move was to find a well driller who was willing to drive his rig out to my property to sink a well at the top of the draw. I was thinking that if we could tap into the existing water table that fed the spring and go deeper I might be able to get a better flow for a longer period of time. It was late June when the well driller arrived and set up at the top of the draw. We drilled for 133 feet (remember that we were sitting on top of a 40 dike of basalt.) when we hit water. Not a lot of water but we had flow. The best part was because of the rock I didn't need to invest in a ton of well casing. I used about 40 feet of 4 inch well casing for the well.

Of course now I had some water, the problem was how was I going to get it up. An electric submersible pump was out of the question. Running 20 miles of power line and poles would cost a arm and a leg. Also when some one sees a power line that is a sure indicator that there is something at the end of the power line. (Not a good idea if and when the SHFT) So I spent my week ends cruising the byways or the agricultural areas of the state looking for old Aeromotor windmills. Those old wind mills drove what are called lift pumps. A lift pump is a piston in a cylinder with a valve at the bottom of the cylinder. There is a piston with a valve in it. When crank on the wind mill forces the piston down, that valve at the bottom of the cylinder closes and the water is forced through the valve in the piston. on the up stroke the valve in the piston closes and the valve at the bottom of the cylinder opens to allow water to enter the cylinder. It is simple, efficient and lasts a long time. Of course your piston and cylinder need to match the amount of water you are going to pump. But since I was going to buy stuff that were basically derelicts I didn't have much choice. I finally found an old 12 foot in diameter wind mill on a 50 tower driving a 5/8 inch lift rod into a two and half inch cylinder lift pump. In a 20 mile an hour wind it would pump about 200 gallons an hour or 3 gallons a minute. Of course I didn't think I would get any were near that. Well it took me the rest of the summer to rebuild the wind mill blades, wind mill gear box and arm. While i was on my hunting trip I set up my wind mill set the pump cylinder and let the thing rip. Even in the first week of October after a dry summer, I was getting over a two gallons a gallon a minute from the wind mill.

Once the well was in it was another case were no good deed goes unpunished. I just had to have a place to store the water that the well was pumping. Of course that called for me to build a cistern. Of course in order to build a cistern I need to acquire some heavy equipment. I had to wait until January when they have the annual commercial equipment auctions. But again I tend to get involve in things I have not right to get into. I became the top bidder for a old 1947 Caterpillar D2 crawler Dozer that had seen much better days. To be honest it had one track in the scrap metal salvage yard and the other one was missing. But hey the price was right $2000.00 so I got to spend the rest of the spring and summer scrounging around for parts to get it operational. Come hunting season I loaded the cat on a flat bed trailer and towed it out to what I was now calling RANCHO COSTO MUCHO DINERO. (A little Spanish lingo there) The hunting trip was a total waste of time. "Why was it a waste of time?" you may ask. Because instead of hunting deer I spent all my time running around on that dammed dozer. But I did move a lot of dirt and rock. I even considered trying my hand at farming again. Hell I grew up on a farm in Idaho so it wasn't like I didn't know what I was doing. You do know you can take the boy out of the farm but you can't take the farm out of the boy. Any way I spent the winter researching low water use farming techniques. I found the the Kibbutzes in Israel had developed a lot of ingenious was to grow crops with out using a lot of water. The main thing is the sun and dry air can suck away 25% of the water before it ever reaches the roots of the plant. What the Israelis do is dig a ditch about a foot from the crop rows. This ditch is half filled with course gravel and sand. The ditch is then covered with clay dirt. Then PVC pipe is laid between the rows of crops. Small metal pipes stick out of the bottom of the PVC into the buried gravel. Water us turned on to seep into the ground around the plant roots around midnight. What i planned to do was to put water sensors in the rows of crops. The water sensors would go back to a old laptop PC that would analyze the moisture of the soil. If the plants needed watering a the computer would fire a solenoid to open a valve just after midnight when it was cool to minimize evaporation, and let water run into the gravel. The time the solenoid was open was dependent on the water content of the soil. Since this whole thing was going to be off the grid I built up a solar cell recharging system for a bank of deep cycle lead acid batteries, That would run the computer, sensor net and solenoids.

I took a two week vacation that year and went out to RANCHO COSTO MUCHO DIENRO and constructed the cistern. It turned out pretty well. I blasted a pit 70 feet long 30 feet wide and between 20 to 25 feet deep. The pit was lined with sprayed concrete over chicken wire and then finished with fiberglass resin to make it water proof. The cistern was covered with a concrete roof and about 30 inches of dirt for insulation. The Cistern holds just under a acre foot of water. ( an acre foot is 212X212x1 feet). I saved the rock that was removed from the pit to be used for the building of a rock walled cabin on the property. (The cabin turned out to be really nice. The walls are about a foot thick with thick steel shutters that cover the windows and a thick steel door. When the windows are shuttered the whole cabin is bullet proof. You will have to blast your way in to get in.) Did I say that it is rather heat efficient. A foot of rock takes a long time to heat up. So the coolness of the night will last almost all day.l I also blasted a cave to place the computer water system and solenoids in for the irrigation system. The cave was sealed by a 1 inch thick steel door with internal hinges and a hidden locking bar system.
